paras.text: In cyclopropane (C₃H₆), each carbon atom, like alkanes, is bonded to four other atoms, so it uses sp³-hybrid orbitals to form sigma bonds. However, in this case, the sp³–sp³ overlap of C–C bond is not maximum as in the case of alkanes. This is due to the fact that in cyclopropane the C–C–C bond angle is 60° and not 109.5° (tetrahedral angle) due to which orbitals do not overlap exactly along their axes (Figure.16.2), but overlap outside of inter-nuclear axes, and form bent bonds. The C–C bond of cyclopropane is therefore weaker than C–C bond of alkane, due to less effective overlap of sp³-hybrid orbitals of carbon in cycopropane. The C–H bonds are formed by overlap of sp³-hybrid orbital of carbon and 1s orbital of hydrogen.

paras.text: In cyclopropane, the three carbon atoms occupy the corners of an equilateral triangle, which results in the C–C–C bond angles to be of 60°. Since the hybridization of carbon is sp³, these C–C–C bond angles should be 109.5°. This deviation from the normal tetrahedral angle of 109.5° to 60° causes a strain in molecule, called Angle strain. The H–C–H bond angle is approximately 115° and the C–C and C–H bond lengths are 151 pm and 108 pm respectively.

16.2.3.2 Structure of Cyclopropane

In cyclopropane (C₃H₆), each carbon atom, like alkanes, is bonded to four other atoms, so it uses sp³-hybrid orbitals to form sigma bonds. However, in this case, the sp³–sp³ overlap of C–C bond is not maximum as in the case of alkanes. The C–H bonds are formed by overlap of sp³-hybrid orbital of carbon and 1s orbital of hydrogen.

In cyclopropane, the three carbon atoms occupy the corners of an equilateral triangle, which results in the C–C–C bond angles to be of 60°. Some important terms

1. Electrophile (Electron loving)

A reagent which can accept an electron pair in a reaction is called an electrophile. An electrophile may be positive ion or neutral molecule with an electron-deficient center. Examples are; H⁺, Cl⁺, CH₃⁺, NO₂⁺, AlCl₃, BF₃, SO₃ etc.

2. Nucleophile (Nucleus loving)

A reagent which can donate an electron-pair to an electrophilic center, in a reaction is called a nucleophile. A nucleophile may be negative ion or neutral molecule with lone pair of electrons. Examples are; Cl⁻, OH⁻, CH₃⁻, NH₂⁻, NH₃, H₂O etc.

3. Free Radicals

A free radical is an atom or group of atoms having unpaired electron(s). Free radicals are produced during the homolytic fission of a covalent bond. They are very reactive as they have strong tendency to pair up their unpaired electron with another electron from wherever available. Examples are; H•, Cl•, •CH₃ etc.

4. Homolytic and Heterolytic bond fission

Bond breaking (fission) is an endothermic process. If sufficient amount of energy is available, a covalent bond can undergo fission in two ways.

a) Homolytic Bond Fission or Homolysis: In Homolytic fission, a chemical bond breaks in such a way that each of the two bonded atoms acquires one of the bonding electrons. Homolysis results in the formation of free radicals. The arrows in the following general example shows the movement of one electron each to both atoms.

b) Heterolytic Bond Fission or Heterolysis: In Heterolytic fission the chemical bond breaks in such a way that one of the bonded atoms acquires both of the bonded electrons. The atom with high electronegativity, usually, acquires both the bonding electrons. Heterolysis results in the formation of ions (electrophile and nucleophile). The arrow in the following general example indicates the movement of sigma electrons towards a single atom.

Figure 16.1 Orbitals overlap description in formation of C–C and C–H sigma bonds of ethane.

Self-assessment

Draw orbital hybridization model of propane and show different types of overlaps in formation of carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds.

16.2.3.2 Structure of Cyclopropane

In cyclopropane (C₃H₆), each carbon atom, like alkanes, is bonded to four other atoms, so it uses sp³-hybrid orbitals to form sigma bonds. However, in this case, the sp³–sp³ overlap of C–C bond is not maximum as in the case of alkanes. This is due to the fact that in cyclopropane the C–C–C bond angle is 60° and not 109.5° (tetrahedral angle) due to which orbitals do not overlap exactly along their axes (Figure.16.2), but overlap outside of inter-nuclear axes, and form bent bonds. The C–C bond of cyclopropane is therefore weaker than C–C bond of alkane, due to less effective overlap of sp³-hybrid orbitals of carbon in cycopropane. The C–H bonds are formed by overlap of sp³-hybrid orbital of carbon and 1s orbital of hydrogen.

In cyclopropane, the three carbon atoms occupy the corners of an equilateral triangle, which results in the C–C–C bond angles to be of 60°. Since the hybridization of carbon is sp³, these C–C–C bond angles should be 109.5°. This deviation from the normal tetrahedral angle of 109.5° to 60° causes a strain in molecule, called Angle strain. The H–C–H bond angle is approximately 115° and the C–C and C–H bond lengths are 151 pm and 108 pm respectively.

Figure 16.2 Overlap between sp³-hybrid orbitals of carbon atoms in cyclopropane.

Some important terms

1. Electrophile (Electron loving)

A reagent which can accept an electron pair in a reaction is called an electrophile. An electrophile may be positive ion or neutral molecule with an electron-deficient center. Examples are; H⁺, Cl⁺, CH₃⁺, NO₂⁺, AlCl₃, BF₃, SO₃ etc.

2. Nucleophile (Nucleus loving)

A reagent which can donate an electron-pair to an electrophilic center, in a reaction is called a nucleophile. A nucleophile may be negative ion or neutral molecule with lone pair of electrons. Examples are; Cl⁻, OH⁻, CH₃⁻, NH₂⁻, NH₃, H₂O etc.

3. Free Radicals

A free radical is an atom or group of atoms having unpaired electron(s). Free radicals are produced during the homolytic fission of a covalent bond. They are very reactive as they have strong tendency to pair up their unpaired electron with another electron from wherever available. Examples are; H•, Cl•, •CH₃ etc.

4. Homolytic and Heterolytic bond fission

Bond breaking (fission) is an endothermic process. If sufficient amount of energy is available, a covalent bond can undergo fission in two ways.

a) Homolytic Bond Fission or Homolysis: In Homolytic fission, a chemical bond breaks in such a way that each of the two bonded atoms acquires one of the bonding electrons. Homolysis results in the formation of free radicals. The arrows in the following general example shows the movement of one electron each to both atoms.

b) Heterolytic Bond Fission or Heterolysis: In Heterolytic fission the chemical bond breaks in such a way that one of the bonded atoms acquires both of the bonded electrons. The atom with high electronegativity, usually, acquires both the bonding electrons. Heterolysis results in the formation of ions (electrophile and nucleophile). The arrow in the following general example indicates the movement of sigma electrons towards a single atom.
